document_meta.title: State Wildlife Action Plan for New Mexico 2025

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) for New Mexico, produced by the New Mexico Department of Wildlife, covering 505 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across six Level II ecoregions. The document treats climate change as a central, dedicated theme (Chapter 4), discussing projected changes to temperature, precipitation, and habitats in detail, with an additional new Appendix F devoted to climate vulnerability analysis. With respect to range shifts, the document explicitly addresses species moving northward/upslope, discusses climate refugia at length (including spatially explicit refugia maps and tables by Conservation Opportunity Area), and incorporates a Climate Change Vulnerability Index (CCVI) assessment for 295 vertebrate SGCN. The document incorporates substantial new analyses performed for this revision—including a CCVI-based vulnerability assessment by NRI/Texas A&M, climate refugia identification by USFS RMRS, and SDM-based future habitat modeling by NHNM—alongside references to broader scientific literature.

time_bound_and_monitoring.absence_note: The document mandates a 10-year review cycle (by October 1, 2035) and requires monitoring of effectiveness of conservation actions as a SWG program requirement. However, individual conservation actions in the ecoregion chapters are framed as 'proposed, voluntary conservation actions' without specific deadlines or milestones attached to each. The monitoring chapter discusses approaches but does not specify time-bound effectiveness monitoring protocols for individual actions. This satisfies a general adaptive management principle (score 1) but does not reach score 2, which requires action-level deadlines AND effectiveness monitoring operationalized per action.

projects: CCVI application to 295 vertebrate SGCN by NRI/Texas A&M (NRI 2025): provides directly applicable vulnerability scores for New Mexico SGCN using a validated framework, supporting prioritization of conservation actions.

SDM-based refugia study by NHNM for 10 SGCN within the Jemez Mountains COA (Muldavin 2024): modeled current and future (2075) habitat suitability under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5, showing variable refugia effectiveness across species—providing limited but real evidence that some COAs will serve as climate refugia.

USFS RMRS climate refugia analysis (Friggens et al. 2025): compiled 70+ macro- and microrefugia indicators across watersheds, cross-walked to COAs and ecoregions, providing applied spatial evidence for prioritizing conservation actions.
